summary:
Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in Poland, which stands as the parent framework for Subcarpathian Voivodeship. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals; her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status.

At the voivodeship level the exposure is social rather than statutory. The Subcarpathian Voivodeship council repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution on 20 September 2021, on the same day as the Małopolska and Lubelskie councils, after the European Commission threatened to withhold regional development funds; Subcarpathian Voivodeship replaced the ordinance with a generic anti-discrimination statement. Such documents were declarations of local policy, not criminal statutes, and carried no penalty for visitors.

The county-level era ended in April 2025, when the county of Łańcut, within Subcarpathian Voivodeship, repealed the country's last surviving anti-LGBT resolution at an extraordinary councillors' session. At the peak of the wave, the Atlas of Hate mapping project recorded such documents covering about one third of Poland's territory.

Both the voivodeship repeal and the final county repeal were forced from outside through the threat to regional development funds rather than produced by a change in local attitudes, so the social climate that generated the resolutions is assessed to persist. Harassment exposure remains the operative concern for a visibly trans person at a public event in the county that resisted external pressure until 2025.

The national legal environment is in transition. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.
tangentialFactors:
Subcarpathian Voivodeship was one of three voivodeship councils to surrender an anti-LGBT resolution on 20 September 2021, alongside Małopolska and Lubelskie, indicating that the mechanism was national and financial rather than local. The European Commission's leverage over regional development funds, not domestic litigation or advocacy, produced the change.

Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024, which bears on how quickly the repeal of local declarations translates into changed practice on the ground.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially at national level. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement, a protection mechanism that a trans visitor could in principle trigger after an incident, though its operational reach in Subcarpathian Voivodeship is not documented in the sources.
localsOnly:
Residents of Subcarpathian Voivodeship live under a voivodeship-level anti-discrimination statement adopted in place of the repealed resolution, which does not create a cause of action specific to gender identity.

Poland offers no legal framework recognising same-sex partnerships, a gap the European Court of Human Rights found unlawful in September 2024; the judgment calls for a recognition framework that does not yet exist, so couples have no standing route to hospital-visit, inheritance or next-of-kin rights.

Trans residents in custody have no specialised prison section to apply to. Placement is decided case by case, and the July 2024 European Court of Human Rights judgment confirms that denial of hormone replacement therapy is actionable with damages, but does not guarantee supply in any given facility.

Planned extensions of hate-speech protection to gender identity and sexual orientation, and the associated Penal Code penalty increases, were still working their way through the legislative process in late 2024; the Prosecutor General's special response team and its guidelines for law enforcement are the enforcement machinery currently in place.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the March and October 2024 hate-speech bills at the time of travel is unresolved in the sources and should be verified against the current parliamentary record rather than assumed to be in force.

Whether the social climate in Subcarpathian Voivodeship has shifted since the 2021 repeal is not sourced. The record establishes that the repeal followed a funding threat, and the persistence of local attitudes is an assessment, not a measured finding.

The content and legal effect of the generic anti-discrimination statement adopted by Subcarpathian Voivodeship in place of its resolution is not set out in the sources; whether it names gender identity is unresolved.

No source in this inventory documents trans-specific facilities, healthcare access or incident data within Subcarpathian Voivodeship itself; the detention and care findings are national cases and are presented as the parent framework.
